judge_assessment.explanation: Every claim the judge made holds. I re-derived all eight answers from worksheet.tex and verify.json: problem 1 is two rows of three buttons (3+3=6); problem 2 is a tally bundle plus two singles beside the word card 'seven' (5+2=7); problem 3 is a full five-frame plus four loose counters (5+4=9, the circled word 'nine'); problem 4 compares the numeral 8 against a five-frame plus one (8 > 6); problem 5 is 10+3=13; problem 6 is the word 'twelve' against a full ten-frame plus two (10+2=12); problem 7 is 'eleven' against a full ten-frame plus four (11 < 14); problem 8 is the sixteen error-analysis item (10+6=16). The judge's list '6, 7, 9, 8>6, 13, 12, 11<14, 16' matches item for item, and the ten-frame, tally and word representations really are mutually consistent. Where I part company is answer_key_quality 4/4: the delivered answer_key.pdf's Quick Answers bank prints '4. —' and '7. —' for the two compare problems even though verify.json records both as verified relations ('>' and '<'), and this key contains no manual items at all, so both em dashes are false blanks. final_response.md advertises the bank 'for fast checking' and states that the > / < answers 'are checked as relations rather than numbers' — the artifact the reader actually holds contradicts that sentence on two of eight rows. The judge did not open the bank.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 8 closes the sheet with an error-analysis item built on the exact misconception the sheet has been guarding against: Ben writes 6 for a card reading 'sixteen' because he counted only the loose dots. The trap is declared in verify.json (expr '6', value 6), machine-proved distinguishable from 16, and printed in the key's common-wrong-answer block, so the item teaches the error rather than merely catching it.

The 'full frame means you may start there' move is introduced in the header box and then re-used with escalating demand in problems 3 (five-frame), 5 (ten-frame + 3), 6 (ten-frame + 2 against a word card) and 8 (two frames), so the same idea does the work at four difficulty levels instead of four unrelated skeletons.

The answer key's per-problem 'Listen for:' lines name a specific observable child behaviour ('a child who restarts at one on the second row', 'Card B is more because I can see the dots'), which is coaching an adult can act on rather than a restated answer.

root_causes.description: render_quick_answers._fmt formats a string expected by calling bare sympy.sympify and returns the literal '---' on SympifyError. A relation answer ('>' or '<') is a string that sympify cannot parse, so both verified compare problems fall into the same fallback that render_entry uses for a manual-only problem. The bank therefore encodes 'verified relation' and 'nobody checked this' with the same glyph, and the loss is invisible to every gate — quick-answers reported PASS in gate_log.txt.
evidence: evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-003/answer_key.pdf page 1 Quick Answers prints '4. —' and '7. —' alongside '1. 6', '2. 7', '3. 9', '5. 13', '6. 12', '8. 16'.
evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-003/verify.json ids 4 and 7 are type 'compare', order 'relation', expected '>' and '<' — both verified, neither manual.

scripts/render_quick_answers.py _fmt: the isinstance(v, str) branch returns '---' on (SympifyError, SyntaxError, TypeError, ValueError), the same string render_entry returns for a problem with no expected values.

evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-003/final_response.md claims the comparison problems' '> / < answers are checked as relations rather than numbers', which the delivered bank does not show.

improvements.title: Quick Answers must typeset a verified relation instead of the manual-only em dash
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, handle relation expecteds before the sympify fallback in _fmt: when a problem entry is type 'compare' with order 'relation', map the expected string '<', '>', '=', '<=', '>=', '!=' onto its LaTeX glyph ($<$, $>$, $=$, $\le$, $\ge$, $\ne$) and, where the compare 'values' are literals, print the resolved comparison (e.g. '$12 < 15$') so the bank row carries the same information as the worked solution. Reserve '---' exclusively for problems whose only entries are type 'manual', and add a build warning when _fmt would emit '---' for a non-manual entry, so a future silent drop is loud. Keep this fix separate from the sympify-sandbox fix (quick-answers-must-not-typeset-python-builtins) — that one must REJECT a non-mathematical object, this one must RENDER a relation.
improvements.regression_test: Add to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py a fixture verify JSON holding one {'id':1,'type':'compare','order':'relation','expected':'<'} entry and one {'id':2,'type':'manual','desc':...} entry, then assert the generated bank contains a typeset '<' on row 1 and '---' on row 2, and that row 1 is not '---'. Today row 1 renders '---' (sympify('<') raises SympifyError and _fmt falls through), so the assertion fails before the fix and passes after. Cases in this run that the test reproduces: curr-003 problems 4 and 7.
improvements.expected_impact: Every verified inequality/equality answer becomes visible in the answer key's fast-checking bank, and the em dash regains its single meaning ('nobody machine-checked this'), so a grader can tell a verified relation from a genuine manual item at a glance.
improvements.risk: Low. The change is confined to formatting one expected value; existing numeric, list and dict rows are untouched. The only visible difference is that rows previously blank now print a glyph, which can widen a bank column and re-flow column_count — worth asserting the column arithmetic in the same test.

case_summary: An accurate, well-paced representations workshop for K/1. All eight problems materially exercise the requested focus — every item puts at least two of {picture, numeral, number word} side by side — and I confirmed each answer independently from worksheet.tex against verify.json and the key: 6, 7, 9, 8>6, 13, 12, 11<14, 16. The study guide teaches the focus properly (three sections, each a rule, a worked example and a distinct try-it, all six study-guide checks verified), and the closing error-analysis item is the sheet's best problem. One real defect, missed by the judge: the answer key's Quick Answers bank prints an em dash for the two verified relation answers, which is the same glyph reserved for unchecked manual items, so a grader using the bank cannot tell that problems 4 and 7 were checked at all. The worked solutions do state 'Card A > Card B' and 'Sam < Nina', so the information is recoverable — the loss is confined to the fast-checking bank and to the accuracy of final_response.md's claim about it.
